newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa rand/bonds closing report.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa rand/bonds closing report.

text.p: The dollar's retreat from a fresh eight-year high, coupled with the liquidation of long dollar positions helped the rand recoup some lost ground on Tuesday after it initially weakened nearly three cents.
At 1410 GMT it was trading at 4.6715/6745 against the greenback, having traded as high as 4.6810 bid at one stage, from 4.6530/6580 at 1400 GMT on Tuesday.
The currency began the day under pressure from a large local import order as well as continued offshore demand for dollars as the U.S. currency maintained its inexorable assault on the Deutschmark
"We saw the rand ticking up from 4.6550 in the morning as the dollar rose to higher levels and people bought dollars," a dealer said, adding that stop losses had been triggered as the rand weakened.
The dollar briefly broke above 1.89 against the mark in London earlier -- its highest level since October 1989 -- but had retreated to around 1.8780 by late local trade.
"With the dollar coming back people on long side sold it down again," the dealer said, adding that players looking to avoid weekend carry costs had also cut their longs.
A contributing factor to the rand's recovery was the fact that bond yields had also retreated from their intraday highs, she added.

The dollar's sturdiness meant the rand remained stable against the mark and yen -- it was last quoted at 0.4017/4021 marks from 0.4035/4040 on Tuesday and at 25.4695/4966 yen from 25.5643/5915 yen previously.
Cable's collapse to below 1.60 also helped the rand gain almost 10 cents against the British unit on the day. It was last at 7.4668/4763 from 7.5731/5826 overnight.
On Thursday, dealers said the rand/dollar's movements would depend on the dollar's performance.

"Tomorrow, I think because the rand is looking on the weaker side and ...the trend is still for stronger dollar, people will look to buy on any dip," a dealer said, predicting a 4.67 to 4.70 range for the rest of the week.
On the bond market, institutional buying coupled with jobber short-covering helped the R150 retrace from its high to trade stronger late on Wednesday.
At 1410 GMT it was pegged at a 14.06 percent yield from 14.145 percent on Tuesday after hitting an intraday high of 14.18 percent.
"It looks like there was a shortage of stock at the higher levels and one or two institutions were buying," a dealer said.
The main factor on most people's minds was Thursday's options close-out, although camps had appeared evenly divided over which way the market would go.
"I think there is a lot related to close-out still in market. It really was a toss of the coin at 14.15 if we would push up to 14.25 or pull down to 14.00 percent," a broker said.

She said the strong diversity of opinion ranged from bearishness about the weaker rand and the potential of foreign profit-taking to bullishness about the fact that there was still momentum in the market and institutional demand at the higher levels.
Dealers were unwilling to predict the market's direction on Thursday ahead of the noon-close out.
Bond Exchange statistics showed foreigners sold a net 89.06 million rand's worth of South African bonds on Tuesday after selling 38.34 million rand's on Monday.
Turnover was 8.8 billion rand compared with Monday's 9.65 billion rand.
The South African Reserve Bank said the money market shortage rose to 7.985 billion rand on Tuesday from 7.537 billion rand on Monday.
Offered rates for three-month NCDs were steady at between 15.40 to 15.50 percent, while the 90-day BA rate was also unchanged at 14.90 percent.
-- Paul Richardson, Johannesburg newsroom 27 11 482 1003
